data.title: Erysipelas and cellulitis — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 14 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erysipelas and cellulitis** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define erysipelas and cellulitis; how do they differ?**
- Erysipelas: infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics — bright red, raised, shiny plaque with a sharp, palpable advancing edge
- Cellulitis: infection of deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat — poorly demarcated, not raised, warm tender swelling
- Erysipelas is mostly Streptococcus pyogenes (group A; also B, C, G); cellulitis is streptococcal and S. aureus; both may coexist

**Q2. Common sites and portals of entry?**
- Legs now commonest (previously face); face erysipelas often butterfly-like, may follow nasal/ear lesion
- Portals: toe-web tinea/intertrigo (most important), leg ulcers, eczema, trauma, insect bites, surgical wounds, venepuncture
- Predisposing: lymphoedema (post-mastectomy, filariasis), venous insufficiency, obesity, diabetes, alcoholism, previous episode, saphenous vein harvest

**Q3. Clinical features?**
- Prodrome of fever, chills, malaise (often precedes rash by hours)
- Red, hot, tender, oedematous area; may have blisters, haemorrhage, lymphangitic streaks, tender regional nodes
- Erysipelas: 'peau d'orange' surface, sharp edge; ear involvement (no deep dermis there) favours erysipelas — Milian's ear sign

**Q4. What is Milian's ear sign?**
- Ear involvement in facial erysipelas; it helps differentiate erysipelas from deep cellulitis since the ear has no subcutaneous fat

**Q5. Discuss the differential diagnosis.**
- Bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis — think venous (stasis) dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, contact dermatitis
- DVT, acute gout, erythema nodosum, early necrotising fasciitis, herpes zoster (prodrome), fixed drug eruption, insect bite reaction, eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells), erythema migrans, lupus (malar), angioedema

**Q6. What are the red flags for necrotising fasciitis? (short note topic)**
- Pain out of proportion to the visible signs; rapid spread; woody hardness of subcutis beyond the erythema; dusky/grey discoloration, haemorrhagic bullae; anaesthesia of skin; crepitus; systemic toxicity, shock
- Type I polymicrobial (diabetics, perineum — Fournier's gangrene), type II group A strep ± S. aureus, type III Vibrio/clostridial
- LRINEC score helps; diagnosis is surgical (finger test — no resistance, dishwater pus); needs urgent debridement + broad IV antibiotics (including clindamycin to switch off toxin)

**Q7. Investigations?**
- Mainly clinical; CBC, CRP, blood sugar, renal function
- Blood culture if systemic toxicity; swab only if open wound/blister
- ASO/anti-DNase B retrospectively; Doppler to exclude DVT; X-ray/MRI if osteomyelitis or gas suspected; creatine kinase high in necrotising infection

**Q8. How do you treat?**
- Mild: oral penicillin V / amoxicillin, or cloxacillin/cephalexin (covers staph) for 5–10 days; clindamycin or macrolide if penicillin allergy
- Moderate–severe: IV benzylpenicillin + cloxacillin, or cefazolin/ceftriaxone; vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA
- Leg elevation, rest, analgesia; treat toe-web tinea and other portals; mark the edge to monitor

**Q9. How do you prevent recurrence?**
- Treat interdigital tinea, control oedema (compression), weight loss, skin care, treat venous disease
- For ≥2 episodes/year: prophylactic penicillin V 250 mg twice daily (PATCH trial) or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU every 3–4 weeks
- Erythromycin for allergic patients

**Q10. Complications?**
- Recurrence (in about 1/3) leading to lymphoedema — elephantiasis nostras verrucosa
- Abscess, necrotising fasciitis, septicaemia, toxic shock, glomerulonephritis, thrombophlebitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis (facial)

**Q11. Name special forms of cellulitis.**
- Perianal streptococcal dermatitis (children; bright red perianal rash, painful defecation)
- Blistering distal dactylitis (group A strep, fingertip pulp blister)
- Haemophilus influenzae facial cellulitis (bluish-purple, unvaccinated children)
- Animal bites: Pasteurella multocida (rapid onset within 24 h) — amoxicillin-clavulanate
- Water exposure: Aeromonas (freshwater), Vibrio vulnificus (seawater, liver disease)
- Orbital/periorbital cellulitis — emergency

**Q12. What is eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells syndrome)?**
- Recurrent cellulitis-like red indurated plaques, not infective, with dermal eosinophils and 'flame figures'; triggers — insect bites, drugs, infections; responds to steroids, not antibiotics

**Q13. What is erysipeloid?**
- Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae from handling fish, meat, poultry — violaceous, well-defined plaque on the hand/finger with central clearing, sparing terminal phalanx; penicillin

**Q14. What is scarlet fever? (short note)**
- Group A strep producing erythrogenic (pyrogenic) toxin, usually from tonsillitis in children
- Fine sandpaper-like punctate erythema starting on neck/upper trunk, Pastia's lines in flexures, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue (white then red), later desquamation of palms/soles
- Penicillin 10 days; complications: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

## Quick spotter facts
- Sharp raised edge + ear involved = erysipelas
- Pain out of proportion + anaesthetic skin + crepitus = necrotising fasciitis — surgical emergency

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
